thread.title: Micron: First Price Fixing, Now Antitrust Allegations By The Chinese Government - Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)

author: Robert Castellano
title: Micron: First Price Fixing, Now Antitrust Allegations By The Chinese Government - Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU)

organizations.name: anti-monopoly bureau of ministry of commerce

text:
On April 27, 2018, Micron Technology ( MU ), along with Samsung Electronics ( OTC:SSNLF ) and SK Hynix ( OTC:HXSCL ), were sued for alleged DRAM price fixing. The class action lawsuit alleges that Samsung, Hynix, and Micron conspired to limit the supply of memory, keeping consumer prices artificially high as a result.
According to the complaint filed by the law firm of Hagens Berman :
“Defendants combined and contracted to fix, raise, maintain, or stabilize the prices at which DRAM was sold in the United States from at least June 1, 2016 to February 1, 2018 (the “Class Period”). Defendants’ conspiracy artificially inflated prices for DRAM throughout the supply chain that were ultimately passed through to Plaintiffs and the Class, causing them to pay more for DRAM Products than they otherwise would have absent Defendants’ conspiracy.”
Now new data will add more ammunition to the litigation against MU. On May 25, 2018, less than a month later, we learned that antitrust officials from China’s Anti-Monopoly Bureau of Ministry of Commerce met with Micron Technology yesterday to “express concerns” about continued price increases for PC DRAM products.
I have been an expert witness in several litigation and this allegation, along with China’s National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) meeting with Samsung on the price issues, could have a detrimental impact on the class action suit.
According to the data of TrendForce :
“China has become the largest importer of memory products, consuming 20% of DRAM and 25% of NAND all over the world. In the recent years, the Chinese government has been actively building up domestic DRAM and NAND Flash industries. However, this cannot cope with the cost pressure immediately since it will take at least a couple of quarters for China to realize independent R&D in technology and stabilize the scale of mass production.
Earlier this year, China’s National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) got involved in the DRAM pricing by meeting with Samsung on the price issues. Currently, there is no evidence that the two meetings are related, but it is obvious that the Chinese government has been very attentive to the price upswing of DRAM.
In addition, Micron had previously interfered with the supplying of upstream equipment to JHICC in contravention to the spirit of fair competition.”
Let’s Discuss Record Operating Margins DRAMeXchange’s article also noted that the three DRAM suppliers have all pushed their respective operating margins significantly to the level of 50-70%, the highest record in history, exceeding that in Application Processor, which is more technically advanced.
I addressed the operating margins of the three companies in several Seeking Alpha articles. The latest, in an April 28, 2018 article entitled “Micron Technology Keeps Rolling With The Punches Despite Headwinds,” and I’ve copied the pertinent chart (Chart 1) below:
Chart 1
Chart 2 below shows a direct correlation between MU’s stock price and DRAM spot price. But it also shows a correlation with MU’s Operating Profit Margin shown in Chart 1. The company’s OP Margin moved from negative to positive between Q1 and Q2, and the company’s stock price started increasing in the same period.
Chart 2
Operating Profit Margin Vs. Bit Growth Solid State Technology published an article in March 2018 entitled, “Are the major DRAM suppliers stunting DRAM demand?”, stating:
“In 2017, DRAM bit volume growth was 20%, half the 40% rate of increase registered in 2016. For 2018, each of the three major DRAM producers (e.g., Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron) have stated that they expect DRAM bit volume growth to once again be about 20%. However, monthly year-over-year DRAM bit volume growth averaged only 13% over the nine-month period of May 2017 through January 2018.”
Chart 3 shows the increase in DRAM bit growth, according to The Information Network’s report entitled “Global Semiconductor Equipment: Markets, Market Shares, Market Forecasts.”
Chart 3

Investor Takeaway The operating margins shown by Micron Technology are welcome news for investors and traders. However, when placed in the context of:
a price fixing class action lawsuit, discussions between the Chinese government and Samsung on DRAM pricing, and discussions between the Chinese government and Micron on DRAM pricing... ...it raises questions.
DRAMeXchange explained that:
“The growth of DRAM supply slowed down over the past two years due to major manufacturers' production control and problems that stemmed from a transition into ten-nanometer process. As a result, the average price of a 4GB DDR4 DRAM module for PCs which stood at US$13 at the end of the second quarter of last year, shot up 130% to US$30.5 in the fourth quarter of this year.”
And it also raises the question: are we consumers paying more for products and thereby rewarding incompetent management and engineering? For example, in an April 4, 2018 article :
“In late March, Micron reported that its production facility Micron Memory Taiwan (formerly Rexchip) experienced an interruption of nitrogen gas supply due to the malfunctioning of the gas generation system located outside the facility, according to DRAMeXchange, a division of TrendForce. Although the equipment has been fixed, the facility is not expected to return to full operation until early April. This will likely cause a hiccup in supply and higher price hikes, but it should be temporary and not last through the second quarter.
This is the second shut down of a Micron fab facility in one year due to a nitrogen gas equipment malfunction. In July 2017, Micron Technology Taiwan’s Fab-2 was shut down due to the malfunction of a nitrogen gas dispensing system that contaminated the wafers and equipment at the facility. It caused a production capacity loss of around 60,000 wafers out of a total of 125,000 wafer starts per month.”
So, engineering has trouble with transitions, and also allows malfunctioning gas systems TWICE at the same plant in a year, thereby disrupting production, which in turn decreases supply, increases prices, and increases stock values (Chart 2). Since management hires the engineering team, they too can be considered incompetent to allow this to happen TWICE.
On another note, I’d like to welcome my new best friend Joe Moore of Morgan Stanley to the group of most disliked people on the MU SA thread, which includes myself, Notable Calls (read report here ), Applied Materials ( AMAT ) CEO Gary Dickerson (read report here ), Apple ( AAPL ) CFO Luca Maestri (read report here ), and last but not least Timothy Arcuri of UBS (read report here ).
Joseph Moore downgraded Micron from Overweight to Equal Weight, noting that DRAM remains strong, but that strength looks priced in and shares have approached his $65 price target, a 4% upside to yesterday’s close. The stock was down 8% on Thursday, more than wiping out the stock price gain from Micron’s $10 billion stock buyout a week earlier.
If MU loses the class action lawsuit, it will be a blip in the company’s revenue. But the political fallout could be disastrous for the company in the long term. As many as five Chinese memory suppliers are coming out with products in the next nine months. The sour taste in the mouths of memory buyers across the globe who have been raped and pillaged will be remembered when Chinese capacity comes on stream.
China’s JHICC and Innotron have been developing 22nm DRAM. According to an article in EETimes, JHICC is sampling DRAM products at 22nm, similar to Micron’s 20nm process (see Chart 4 below, which incidentally is six months behind SSNLF). Indeed, the Chinese DRAM startup is expected to ramp 10,000 to 20,000 wafer starts per month (WSPM) of capacity in the third quarter this year. That figure would put JIHCC at about 1.5% of global wafer starts, according to the article.
Chart 4
While initially small, it will change the supply-demand dynamics sufficiently to result in DRAM price drops, which all the above members of the disliked people on the MU SA thread have been saying. Charts 5 and 6 illustrate these drops in prices.
Chart 5
Chart 6
Chart 5 forecasts that NAND ASP price changes for Samsung Electronics, which moved into negative territory in Q1 2018, will continue to drop through the remainder of 2018. For DRAMs, KIS forecasts that ASPs should continue to demonstrate positive growth for Q2 2018, but will drop significantly starting in Q3 ending September 2018.
Chart 6 presents a similar analysis for MU by BofA Merrill Edge. NAND ASPs moved into negative territory in Q1 2018 ending November 2017. DRAM ASPs are forecast to move negatively in Q4 2018, ending in August 2018 (the same period as SSNLF).
These forecasts coincide with the introduction of DRAMs by China's JHICC, ramping up output as high as 20,000 wafers per month. The output of the Chinese is sufficient to move the supply of DRAMs into surplus in 2018, as shown in Table 2.

All signs are pointing to a drop in DRAM ASPs starting in Q3 2018 tied to capacity increases coming from bit growth by the existing DRAM suppliers and new capacity coming on stream by JSICC. We are also witnessing similar rhetoric from buyers of DRAMs, such as Apple's CFO Luca Maestri stating he expects NAND and DRAM prices to fall.
In 2019, Chinese DRAM manufacturer Innotron will also be racing up production. Then of course, we will continue to see DRAM bit growth by existing suppliers. Samsung's Line 16, which was initially designed for 2D NAND, will be turned into a DRAM line to pick up the slack from Line 11’s CMOS Image Sensor conversion. The P1 plant, which is ramping production to 50,000 wpm in 2018, has a capacity estimated at 130,000 wpm (30,000 wpm for the second floor of the West Building and 100,000 wpm for the East Building).
We are witnessing a great deal of volatility in MU's stock, and every analysis or comment I described above (UBS, Morgan Stanley, Notable Calls, AMAT, AAPL) has resulted in significant stock price drops. We witnessed just today a significant 2.5% drop merely on rumors that the Chinese government raided MU's China offices. As of this writing, they are unsubstantiated.
MU's stock run has been directly correlated with ASPs (Chart 2). If DRAM ASPs drop as anticipated, I expect a similar reaction in the stock price.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
